stories.title: Volcano Ash Grounds Planes Between Singapore and Jakarta!
stories.headline_kid: A volcano in Indonesia erupted and its ash cloud caused flight chaos at Changi Airport!
summary: Mount Anak Krakatau, a volcano in Indonesia, erupted over the weekend and shot huge clouds of ash high into the sky. Volcanic ash is made of tiny, sharp bits of rock and glass — if a plane flies through it, the ash can clog and damage the engines. That is why airlines quickly cancel or delay flights whenever ash is in the air.

The eruption caused chaos at both Changi Airport in Singapore and Soekarno-Hatta Airport in Jakarta. Some travellers turned up at Changi only to discover their flight had already been grounded. Meanwhile, some passengers in Jakarta had already gone through immigration checks — only to be told to turn back!

In total, more than 900 flights were affected, and eight airports in the region had to pause their operations. Singapore Airlines was one of the airlines caught up in the mess, along with several others flying between Singapore and Indonesia.

This shows how a natural event thousands of kilometres away can suddenly disrupt travel plans for thousands of people. Airlines are now working to clear the backlog of delayed passengers and rebook flights as soon as it is safe to fly again.

lenses.me: If your family is flying to or from Indonesia soon, your trip might get delayed — always good to check flight status before heading to the airport.
lenses.family: Parents planning a holiday to Bali or Jakarta may need to change their plans or claim refunds for cancelled flights.
lenses.friends: Classmates who were supposed to go on a school trip or family holiday to Indonesia this week may have exciting (or annoying!) stories to share.
lenses.nation: Changi Airport, one of the world's busiest airports, had to manage a sudden wave of confused and frustrated travellers.
lenses.world: It shows how connected air travel is — one volcano can ripple out to affect flights across an entire region.

stories.title: Singapore Police Help Nepal Find Its Missing
stories.headline_kid: Singapore sent special police experts to help Nepal identify people who died in its terrible floods.
summary: Three weeks ago, a huge collapse of glacier and rock on the China-Nepal border caused massive flooding, sweeping away homes and roads. At least 1,385 people have died, and nearly 4,900 people are still missing — that's almost the size of a whole town gone silent.

Because so many bodies are hard to identify after being buried in mud and debris, Singapore has sent forensic police specialists to Nepal to help. Forensic experts use science — like fingerprints, dental records and DNA — like detectives solving a puzzle, so families can finally learn what happened to their loved ones.

The work is extremely tough. Rescuers are searching in unstable, muddy terrain that could collapse again at any moment. But there have been small miracles too — a Nepali woman and a Chinese hydropower worker were both pulled out alive after being trapped for 10 days.
These rare survival stories have given rescuers new hope, even as the difficult and heartbreaking search for the missing continues.

lenses.me: It shows how even kids your age can grow up to do important jobs like forensic science, helping bring comfort to grieving families.
lenses.family: Your family might talk about how lucky we are to be safe, and think about ways to help disaster victims, like donating to relief funds.
lenses.friends: You and your classmates might discuss how it feels when something scary happens to people far away, and why helping others matters.
lenses.nation: Singapore is recognised for the skills and kindness we contribute during disasters overseas, strengthening our friendship with other countries.
lenses.world: It shows how countries work together during hard times, sharing skills and resources to help one another.

stories.title: Singapore's Stock Market Welcomes More New Companies
stories.headline_kid: More companies are choosing to join the Singapore stock market this year — great news for our economy!
summary: The Singapore Exchange, or SGX, is like a giant marketplace where companies can sell small pieces of themselves, called shares, to raise money to grow. When a company does this for the very first time, it's called an IPO — an Initial Public Offering.

This year, SGX has seen a 'bumper crop' of IPOs, meaning many more companies than usual have chosen to list here in the first half of the year. Experts believe this trend could keep growing if the market stays strong.

Other Asian stock markets, like Hong Kong's, have had even bigger booms with more companies listing. But analysts say Singapore is focusing on quality over quantity — attracting fewer but more valuable companies, rather than trying to win by sheer numbers.

A strong stock market matters because it can create more jobs, boost confidence in our economy, and even affect how much money grows in things like CPF-linked investments that our parents rely on for retirement.

lenses.me: Understanding how the stock market works now will help you make smarter money decisions when you grow up.

lenses.friends: Classmates whose parents work in banking or finance may talk about how busy things are at their jobs.
lenses.nation: A thriving stock market strengthens Singapore's position as one of Asia's top financial centres.
lenses.world: Singapore is competing with markets like Hong Kong and Malaysia to attract the best companies to list their shares.

stories.title: Yummy New Mooncakes to Try This Mid-Autumn Festival!
stories.headline_kid: Mid-Autumn Festival is coming, and Singapore's bakeries have cooked up exciting new mooncake flavours!
summary: Mid-Autumn Festival, an old tradition celebrated by Chinese communities around the world, is coming up soon. Families gather under the full moon, light lanterns, and share mooncakes — round pastries that represent togetherness and reunion, just like the moon's round shape.

This year, Singapore's bakeries and hotels have gone all out with creative new flavours. There are tea-infused mooncakes, cooling snow skin versions, custard-filled treats, and even classic Teochew-style flaky pastries loved by grandparents for generations.

Some bakeries have also created elaborate gift sets, perfect for giving to relatives, teachers, or neighbours during the festive season. It's a chance to try something new while keeping old traditions alive.
Whatever your family's favourite mooncake flavour, the festival is really about spending time together — a reminder that even small traditions can bring big smiles.

lenses.me: You might get to try a brand-new mooncake flavour with your family this year!
lenses.family: Mid-Autumn Festival is a lovely excuse for your family to gather, light lanterns, and share stories.
lenses.friends: You and your classmates from different backgrounds can share how your own families celebrate festivals with food and traditions.
lenses.nation: The festival shows Singapore's multicultural society coming together to celebrate shared traditions.
lenses.world: Mid-Autumn Festival is celebrated in many countries, including China, Vietnam, and South Korea, each with its own special customs.

stories.title: Indonesia Wants Its People Living Abroad to Come Home
stories.headline_kid: Indonesia is thinking about letting some of its citizens living overseas hold two passports, to bring their skills home.
summary: Indonesia's President Prabowo Subianto is considering a new plan: allowing some Indonesians living overseas to hold dual citizenship, meaning they could keep their Indonesian passport as well as citizenship of the country where they now live. Right now, Indonesia usually does not allow this.

The idea is to attract 'diaspora talent' — skilled Indonesians living abroad, like doctors, engineers, and business owners — who could return to help build their home country. Millions of Indonesians live and work overseas, including many right here in Singapore.

This matters for Singapore because we have a large community of Indonesian friends, classmates and workers. Some may have given up their Indonesian citizenship to become Singapore citizens or permanent residents — this new rule could let them reconnect their roots.
However, some people wonder if this plan alone is enough to convince talented Indonesians to actually move back, since jobs, salaries and lifestyle also matter a lot when deciding where to live.

lenses.family: If your family has Indonesian relatives, this news could change how they think about living between two countries.
lenses.friends: Friends with Indonesian heritage might have interesting family stories to share about this topic.
lenses.nation: Singapore's close ties with Indonesia, our nearest neighbour, could grow even stronger through such people-to-people connections.
lenses.world: It's part of a bigger global trend where countries compete to attract talented people to help their economies grow.
